title: Sister recalls dead man as 'a hoot'
subtitle: Robert (Bobby) Bagnell died after being hit by a Taser as police tried to subdue him
article: He was known to police as an "aggressive panhandler" who dabbled in petty crimes -- and, lately, as the 44-year-old man who died after being shot by police with a Taser stun gun.
The family of Robert Wayne Bagnell prefers to remember "Bobby" differently.
"He was crazy, he was a hoot. He had a great sense of humour, loved people," said Bagnell's younger sister, Patti Gillman. "He laughed about everything, because he thought that life was a hoot."

Bagnell's life came to an abrupt end June 23, when a Taser that delivers a 50,000-volt shock was used to subdue him while he was in what police say was a cocaine-induced frenzy. He stopped breathing and was pronounced dead at the scene.

Vancouver police kept the details of the incident secret for a month -- even his family, who live in Ontario and Prince Edward Island, didn't find out he had been shot with a Taser until the news broke Friday on television.
"I was floored. I was stunned, mostly for not having been told," Gillman said. "We should have known before the rest of the world, I think."

The oversight has brought an apology from the Vancouver police department, which claims the family wasn't told initially about the Taser being used because the police report wasn't completed when they were contacted.

"It's our regret that they \[the family\] were not given that information as the investigation continued," Const. Sarah Bloor said. "Sadly, in the course of the duty I guess we didn't call them back to advise them of that and our apologies for that."
Bloor added: "Our sympathies are extended to them and we apologize for our neglect in \[not\] telling them the additional information when we obtained it."
To Gillman, it was just another oversight of the kind that continually dogged the older brother she describes as a "military brat" who fell through the cracks.
"We do really want people to see that he was a human being and that he had people who cared about him," Gillman said from her home in Trenton, Ont.
Bagnell was born in Saskatoon, but "Our dad was in the air force, so we moved around every few years," Gillman recalls.
Bagnell had medical problems at a young age. A military doctor misdiagnosed him as being epileptic, and he took epilepsy medication for years. But the real problem was with his heart.
"He had a hole in his heart, basically," Gillman said, noting that doctors in Montreal finally treated him in 1974.
